title: A Little, Enough, Quite a Lot

lessons.title: थोडा (thoḍā) — a little, some
lessons.gloss: a little, some — the quantity word, which agrees, where जरा the degree word does not

segments.text: जरा softens an adjective. It cannot measure out a quantity of something: jarā water is not Marathi.

segments.instruction: say jarā kaṭhīṇ, then double a word to strengthen it
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: say *jarā kaṭhīṇ*, then double a word to strengthen it]

segments.text: थोडा — thoḍā — a little, some, a small amount of.
थोडं पाणी — thoḍaṁ pāṇī — a little water.

The ending is where the difference lives. थोडा (thoḍā) ends in -आ, so it agrees: थोडा (thoḍā) चहा (masculine), थोडं पाणी (neuter). जरा never changes. The two are close in meaning and behave in opposite ways, and the reason is that they are different parts of speech — थोडा (thoḍā) measures a NOUN, जरा softens an adjective or a verb.
थोडा (thoḍā) चहा — a little tea. जरा कठीण — slightly difficult.
Its ancestor is Sanskrit स्तोक (stoka), "a little, a drop," worn down through the Prakrits. Hindi's thoṛā is the same word by the same road.
Against खूप it is the other end of the same scale: खूप पाणी is a lot of water, थोडं पाणी is a little.

segments.instruction: thoḍaṁ pāṇī, thoḍā chahā — and hear the ending move
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *thoḍaṁ pāṇī*, *thoḍā chahā* — and hear the ending move]

segments.instruction: jarā — and hear that it never would
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *jarā* — and hear that it never would]

segments.prompt: Ask for a little water and a little tea, then say there is a lot of water.
acceptedResponses: thoḍaṁ pāṇī; thoḍā chahā; khūp pāṇī āhe
थोडं पाणी थोडा चहा खूप पाणी आहे

feedback.correct: It agreed twice and khūp did not.
feedback.incorrect: pāṇī is neuter and chahā masculine, so thoḍā changes; khūp never does.

segments.text: Which of थोडा (thoḍā) and जरा agrees, and why? (थोडा (thoḍā) — it measures a noun and ends in -आ.) What Sanskrit word is it worn down from? (स्तोक, a drop.)
Sources: Wiktionary: थोडा (thoḍā).

lessons.title: पुरेसा (puresā) — enough
lessons.gloss: enough, sufficient — the answer that ends a transaction, built on a root that means to fill

segments.text: A little and a lot are both amounts. Neither one says the amount is right.
पुरेसा — puresā — enough, sufficient.
पुरेसं पाणी — puresaṁ pāṇī — enough water.
Another -आ word, so it agrees and you already have all three forms: पुरेसा (puresā) चहा, पुरेसं पाणी.

Said on its own it closes a transaction. पुरे! is that's enough, and a Marathi host pouring tea will stop when you say it — which is a more useful thing to own than it sounds, because the alternative is नको, and नको refuses the whole offer rather than the next spoonful.

That पुरे is the word underneath पुरेसा (puresā), and it comes from the Sanskrit root पूर् (pūr-), "to fill." Enough is filled. The same ancient root gives Latin plenus and English full, so the idea has travelled a long way without changing.

segments.instruction: thoḍaṁ, puresaṁ, khūp — three amounts, smallest first

segments.prompt: Say there is enough water, then stop somebody pouring, then refuse the offer entirely.

feedback.correct: Enough, stop, and no thank you.
feedback.incorrect: pure stops the pouring; nako declines the whole offer.

segments.text: What does पुरे stop, and what does नको stop? (पुरे stops the pouring; नको refuses the offer.) What does the root पूर् mean? (To fill.)
Sources: Wiktionary: पुरेसा (puresā).

lessons.title: बराच (barāch) — quite a lot
lessons.gloss: quite a lot, a fair amount — बरा with the emphatic -च stuck on, and you own both halves

segments.text: A little, enough, a lot. There is a step between enough and a lot that Marathi bothers to name.
बराच — barāch — quite a lot, a fair amount, rather.
बरंच पाणी — baraṁch pāṇī — quite a lot of water.

You already own both halves of this word. बरा is the fine, all right of chapter four — the बरं you answer how are you with — and -च is Marathi's little emphatic tail, the one that means precisely that. Glue them together and a fair amount is literally a good-ish bit.
It agrees, because the बरा underneath it ends in -आ: बराच (barāch) चहा, बरंच पाणी.
Set the four amounts in order and the scale is complete:
थोडं a little, पुरेसं enough, बरंच quite a lot, खूप a lot.

segments.instruction: baraṁch pāṇī — quite a lot of water
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *baraṁch pāṇī* — quite a lot of water]

segments.text: What two pieces is बराच (barāch) made of? (बरा and the emphatic -च.) Which of the four amount words does NOT agree? (खूप.)
Sources: Wiktionary: बराच (barāch).

lessons.title: किती मोठं! (kitī moṭhaṁ!) — how big!
lessons.gloss: how big! — the same किती you have asked with since chapter 37, in front of an adjective instead of a noun

segments.text: किती has asked for a number since chapter thirty-seven. Put it in front of an adjective instead of a noun and it stops asking.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: किती with an adjective

segments.text: किती मोठं! — kitī moṭhaṁ! — how big! किती सुंदर! — kitī sundar! — how beautiful!
Same word, different neighbour, different job. In front of a noun — किती भाऊ? — किती asks for a number. In front of an adjective it exclaims, and no number is wanted or given.

Two things tell the listener which one you mean. On the page it is the! you learned in chapter thirty-three, where a question would have carried?. Out loud it is the tune: the exclamation falls at the end where a question rises. Say the pair back to back and hear your own voice do it.
English works exactly this way — how many? against how lovely! — so this is a construction you can feel rather than one you have to install.
The adjective still agrees, and there is nothing else to remember: किती मोठं! (kitī moṭhaṁ!) of a house, किती मोठी! of a room.

segments.instruction: kitī sundar! — and let the voice fall

segments.instruction: kitī bhāū? — and let it rise

segments.prompt: Ask how many brothers, then exclaim how beautiful, and say which mark each one takes.

feedback.correct: A question and an exclamation from one word.
feedback.incorrect: A noun after kitī asks; an adjective after it exclaims.

segments.text: What decides whether किती asks or exclaims? (Whether a noun or an adjective follows it.) Which mark ends the exclamation, and what does the voice do? (!; it falls.)

lessons.title: How much, how strong, and how!
lessons.gloss: a four-step scale of amount, three settings of degree, and one word that both asks and exclaims

segments.text: Two chapters, seven items, and not one of them was an adjective. Name the four amounts in order before you use any of them.
